newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran names candidates for presidential election.
newsitem.headline: Iran names candidates for presidential election.

text.p: Iran's Islamic watchdog group on Wednesday passed judgment on hundreds of people vying for President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's job, rejecting all but four from standing in the country's May 23 election.

The Guardian Council, a body of six clerics and six lawyers reponsible for screening all election candidates, said in a statement reported by the official news agency IRNA only four presidential hopefuls out of 238 had passed scrutiny.

It named them as Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, who is speaker of the Majlis (parliament), Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri, a former intelligence minister, Mohammad Khatami, a former minister of culture and Islamic guidance, and Reza Zavarei, deputy head of the judiciary.
All except Zavarei are Shi'ite Moslem clergymen.
The Guardian Council screened all of the contenders for their allegiance to Iran's religious leadership and Islamic system of government.
The 234 rejected candidates included nine women, one of them the daughter of one of the ayatollahs who led the 1979 Islamic revolution that toppled the Shah, the late Mohammed Reza Pahlevi.

Campaigning is due to start on Saturday for the election to replace Rafsanjani, a 62-year-old pistachio nut farmer and Shi'ite Moslem cleric who must stand down in August after two consecutive four-year terms as president.
The Majlis, where Rafsanjani was formerly speaker, held its last session on Wednesday until May 25 in order to avoid any attempt by the 270 legislators to influence the campaign.
Since his election by a landslide in 1989, Rafsanjani has tried to reconcile Iran's revolutionary ideals with the task of solving daunting economic problems.
These have been aggravated over the last two years by U.S. sanctions aimed at isolating Iran over its alleged involvement in "terrorism" and attempts to acquire nuclear weapons.

Despite the difficulties, Michel Camdessus, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, recently expressed satisfaction with Iran's economic policy and praised it for reviving growth and reducing inflation.
Nateq-Nouri and Khatami are front-runners in the race for the presidency.
Nateq-Nouri is a former interior minister who is backed by most senior clergy and by the majority conservative faction in the Majlis.
Khatami draws support from Islamist left-wingers and a pro-Rafsanjani centrist group of technocrats and top state officials formed last year.

A public opinion poll published in the daily Tehran Times on Wednesday gave 40.8 percent of popular support to Nateq-Nouri, 33.8 percent to Khatami and 8.2 percent to Reyshahri. The remaining 17.2 percent chose other candidates, were undecided or did not respond.

The poll was conducted by the National Centre for Studies and Assessing Public Opinion, which is affiliated to the Ministry of Guidance and Islamic Culture. It surveyed 1,182 residents of the Iranian capital's 20 districts from April 17 to 24.
It found the top three issues that should be given priority by the next president were resolving economic problems, creating job opportunities and solving problems of youth.

Although Rafsanjani is required by the constitution to stand down as president he will continue to continue to wield considerable influence in state affairs as head of a powerful body that will draw up government policies and advise Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
